evals.prompt: I run docs at Ferrocast, a hosted webhook-delivery API. We've shipped 2023.2, 2024.1, 2024.3 and 2025.1 as release names in our changelog, all additive, nothing was ever removed. There's one deployment and every customer calls the same endpoints, no version header, no pinning. Our docs site is a single set. Sales keeps asking why we don't have a version dropdown like the big payments APIs, and our PM wants a docs version per release name so enterprise customers can 'see the docs as of the release they evaluated'. We're on a hosted docs platform that supports versions natively, so it's basically free to turn on. Can you lay out the versioning setup with the dropdown listing those four releases, and tell me what canonical tags we need on the older ones?
evals.expected_output: A latest-only reference with a changelog and upgrade guides carrying history, the four-release dropdown refused because no client can call anything but the current behaviour, history carried by 'added in' stamps, no canonical tags written, and the API version scheme routed to the platform collection.
expectations: Classifies Ferrocast as the 'hosted API, one callable behaviour' class, not the 'several callable versions' class
Recommends a latest-only reference plus a changelog and an upgrade guide per breaking version, not one docs set per release name
Refuses the four-release dropdown on the grounds that no client can call any version except the current behaviour
Names the single callable behaviour (no pinning, no version header, additive-only) as the interview answer that deleted the selector and per-major rungs
Distinguishes the payments-API comparison: that switcher serves account-pinned callable versions, which Ferrocast does not have
Carries release history on the single docs set with 'added in <release>' stamps rather than duplicated pages
Answers the PM's 'docs as of the release they evaluated' need with the changelog and upgrade guides, not with frozen snapshots per release name
Writes no canonical tags and states that search-entry intent is handed to samber/developer-relations-skills@docs-seo
Routes any decision about the API's own version scheme to samber/developer-platform-skills@api-versioning-policy

Rejects 'free to turn on' as a reason, stating that each live version costs a copy of every released-behaviour fix or qualifying backports, and prices it or asks for the monthly doc-fix count to price it
Lists tutorials, concepts and the changelog as content that stays unversioned
Ties the unversioned URL path for current docs to the condition that one supported line with latest-only docs holds

evals.prompt: Quick sanity check before I do this. Marlinspike is our open-source Python ORM. 4.x is current (4.6), 3.x is on LTS with security fixes until next November per our release policy, 2.x ended two years ago. Our docs site serves all three behind a dropdown and analytics say 3.x pages get about 2% of views and 2.x pages about 1%. Our one tech writer is drowning, so I want to go latest-only: delete the 3.x and 2.x docs this sprint, 301 their URLs to the 4.x home page, and tell people to read the changelog if they're on an old version. PyPI stats, if it matters: 3.x is still 38% of downloads because a large web framework pins it. Give me the plan.
evals.expected_output: A plan that keeps 3.x live as a maintained version because it is still supported and heavily installed, freezes 2.x as a static snapshot instead of deleting it, replaces the wholesale 301 with per-page redirects at the removal step only, limits and prices 3.x backports, and uses downloads rather than view share as the evidence.
expectations: Assigns 3.x the `maintained` docs state because it sits in the support table until November, and refuses to delete its docs while supported
States that a docs window narrower than the support window strands supported users
Uses the 38% download share, not the 2% view share, as the evidence of version need, stating that downloads per version outrank docs traffic for this call
Names the pinning web framework as the reason readers stay on 3.x and promotes the selector on that ground
Cites the pandas precedent, where about 2% of views on old-version paths was kept, against the user's reading of 2% as negligible
Assigns 2.x the `frozen` state: static snapshot, banner, never rebuilt, not deletion
Rejects the wholesale 301 to the 4.x home page; any redirect goes per page to the nearest current equivalent
Orders retirement as freeze, banner, redirect, delete last, with `removed` only once no measurable readers remain
Writes a policy table with one row each for 4.x, 3.x and 2.x carrying product status, support end, docs state, next transition with trigger, and backport scope
Limits 3.x backports to security, legal exposure, data loss and upgrade-blocking steps, and prices them in minutes per month using the 10-20% and 10-30 minute figures labelled as baselines
Names the November support end as the trigger that moves 3.x from `maintained` to `frozen`
Addresses the writer's load with the priced backport rule and by taking 2.x out of the build, not with deletion
Hands 2.x's search-entry posture and the redirect list to samber/developer-relations-skills@docs-seo rather than deciding canonical or noindex tags

evals.prompt: Our Docusaurus site for Quillhaven (self-hosted feature-flag server, single Go binary) has 23 versions in the dropdown: every minor from 1.0 to 3.4 plus 'Next'. The docs root shows Next because that's what engineers see right after they merge. A full build is 21 minutes, CI ran out of memory twice last month, and every PR preview builds the whole thing. We version everything, blog and changelog included, because it was easier to drop them in the versioned folder. Supported lines: 3.x (current), 2.x until March; 1.x is dead but a handful of air-gapped customers still run it. Minors never broke an upgrade, only majors did: the config file format changed at 2.0 and at 3.0. Help me get this under control without breaking the thousands of deep links sitting in support tickets and GitHub issues. I'd like to keep every version available.
evals.expected_output: A consolidation from 23 per-minor versions to three line segments with a per-page redirect list, current as the default landing instead of Next, blog and changelog un-versioned, only current, maintained and next built per deploy with 1.x served as a static snapshot, previews restricted, and the release cut written into the checklist.
expectations: Collapses granularity from per-minor to per-major, citing that minors never changed instructions while 2.0 and 3.0 changed the config format
Names the collapsed versions as line segments `3.x`, `2.x`, `1.x`, not release numbers such as `3.4`
Moves the default landing from Next to `current` (3.x), stating that unreleased docs as default document features readers cannot install
Lists each old minor URL pattern with its per-page target in the collapsed line (for example `/2.3/*` to `/2.x/*`), so no ticket or issue link breaks
Un-versions the blog and the changelog and lists them with tutorials and concepts as unversioned content
Builds only `current`, `maintained` and `next` per deploy and serves 1.x as a static snapshot outside the build
Restricts PR previews to `current` and `next` only
Cites the Docusaurus maintainers' guidance to stay under about 10 built versions and archive older ones as immutable deployments, labelled sourced
Assigns 1.x the `frozen` state because air-gapped installs mean the line is still installed, with an 'unsupported' banner and no 'insecure' wording absent a known vulnerability
Names March as the trigger moving 2.x from `maintained` to `frozen`
Places `current` at the versioned line path `/3.x/` behind a `latest` alias, and points stable links in tickets and support replies at the alias
Writes the release cut into the release checklist: old `current` becomes `maintained`, the alias moves, switcher and banners update, `next` becomes `current`
Hands the redirect map and the search-entry column to samber/developer-relations-skills@docs-seo instead of writing canonical or noindex tags

evals.prompt: Can you write the banner copy and the version-switcher spec for Tarnhelm's docs (Java SDK, docs on our own static site)? Versions live: 5.0 beta (what the docs home shows now, since that's where all the action is), 4.x current, 3.x supported, 2.x and 1.x unsupported but still up. Our existing banner on every old page says 'You are viewing an older version. Go to the docs.' and links to the home page; I'd like to reuse it as-is on the 5.0 beta pages too so we don't maintain two. For the dropdown we want all 31 released versions listed, 1.0 through 4.7, because enterprise customers ask for exact versions. And a quality-of-life thing: remember the reader's chosen version in a cookie and send them straight there when they come in from Google. One more note: 2.x has an unpatched CVE in its XML parser.
evals.expected_output: Current as the default landing, one banner per state built from status word, consequence and same-page link, a distinct unreleased banner for the beta, security wording only on the CVE line, a dropdown collapsed to line segments with older versions grouped, the search-visit cookie redirect refused, same-page switching with ancestor fallback, and switcher instrumentation.
expectations: Moves the default landing from the 5.0 beta to 4.x `current`
Refuses to reuse the old-version banner on the beta pages and writes a distinct `next` banner saying the version is unreleased and its features may change or not ship
Rewrites the banner with three parts in order: a status word, the consequence for the reader, and a same-page link to `current`
Replaces the link to the docs home with a same-page link that falls back to the nearest ancestor section when the page no longer exists
Writes a separate banner per state: `maintained` wording for 3.x (supported older release) and `frozen` wording for 1.x (no longer supported, static snapshot)
Uses the 'known security issues' wording only on 2.x, the line with the CVE, and not on 1.x
Collapses the 31-entry dropdown to one entry per line, with 2.x and 1.x grouped under an 'Older versions' heading
Answers the enterprise request for exact versions with 'added in' and 'changed in' stamps or the per-release reference, not with 31 dropdown entries
Rejects the cookie that auto-redirects visitors arriving from search to a remembered version
Specifies that switching opens the same page in the target version and, when it is missing there, the nearest ancestor section with a one-line notice, never the version root or a 404
Shows which versions are supported next to their labels in the switcher
Gives the 5.0 beta a visible label distinct from stable entries, such as Preview or Unreleased
Recommends instrumenting switcher clicks and switcher 404s before treating any selector change as an improvement
Scopes on-site search to the version being read, `current` by default

evals.prompt: We're formalising docs backports for Brackwater, our self-hosted analytics server. Setup: docs are a branch per version. main carries the unreleased 5.3, which is all additive, and builds the 'next' site; 5.x current builds from the release branch; 4.x and 3.x are both supported and both live. We land about 30 doc fixes a month and roughly 80% of them touch behaviour that's already released. Our policy draft says: 'every doc fix that applies to a supported version gets backported to it'. Our standing capacity for docs work is about 3 hours a month on top of writing. Does the policy hold up? And tell me what to put in the PR template.
evals.expected_output: A priced rejection of the draft policy: the current-in-step term alone exceeds the ceiling while current builds from a release branch, so current moves to main with inline 'coming in 5.3' marks, maintained backports are restricted to four grounds, PRs carry backport targets at review time, baselines are labelled and replaced after a month, and the total is compared with the 3-hour ceiling.
expectations: Prices the 'keeping current in step' term as doc fixes × share touching released behaviour × minutes per copy, and shows it is non-zero because `current` builds from the release branch while main carries `next`
Computes that term at about 30 × 80% × 10-30 minutes, roughly 4-12 hours per month, and states it alone exceeds the 3-hour ceiling
Prices the maintained term as fixes × share qualifying × 2 maintained versions × minutes per backport, using the 10-20% and 10-30 minute figures labelled as baselines
Rejects the draft 'every applicable fix to every supported version' policy by showing its priced cost against the 3-hour ceiling
Recommends building `current` from main and marking unreleased 5.3 content inline ('coming in 5.3') instead of running a separate `next` build, because 5.3 is additive
States that once main starts 6.0, `current` branches from the release tag and the first term is priced again
Writes the rule: every released-behaviour fix to `current`; 4.x and 3.x only for security, legal exposure, data loss, or a step that blocks upgrading; `frozen` never
Requires each doc pull request to carry its backport targets at review time, not after merge, and puts that field in the PR template
States that the baseline figures are replaced with measured ones after one month
Compares the priced total with the 3-hour standing ceiling and, if over, freezes 3.x early or switches to per-major frozen
Names the Django practice (latest stable branch only) and the GitLab exception (older releases rarely: legal, security, upgrade-blocking, data loss) as the precedents the rule combines
Warns that an unpriced rule decays into 'backport nothing' within two releases
Adds to the release checklist that 'coming in 5.3' marks convert to 'added in 5.3' at the release cut

evals.prompt: Docs plan for Larkspur, a hosted document-signing API. Clients pin an API version per account with a date header; three dated versions are callable right now (2024-02-01, 2024-10-15, 2025-06-01), older ones were sunset. We also ship four SDKs (TypeScript, Python, Go, Java), each on its own semver, each already with generated reference on its package registry. Product wants the docs site to have a version picker that covers everything: every API date × every SDK version, so a customer on Python SDK 3.2 against API 2024-10-15 sees exactly their combination, including tutorials rewritten for that pair. We're a team of two writers. What's the versioning model?
evals.expected_output: A selector over the reference only, capped at the three callable API dates, with guides and tutorials kept single, SDK reference linked from the registries, the API date named as the component driving the switcher, a compatibility matrix page, the dated scheme itself routed to the platform collection, and the setup priced against two writers.
expectations: Classifies Larkspur as 'hosted API, several callable versions' with the API date, not the SDK version, driving the docs switcher
Caps versioned reference at three entries, the API's concurrent callable count, never the API-date × SDK-version product
Applies the selector to the reference only; tutorials and guides stay a single set with stamps or badges
Refuses to rewrite tutorials per API-date and SDK-version pair, naming it as versioning content that does not differ between lines
Links the registry-hosted per-release SDK reference from every docs version instead of rebuilding SDK reference on the docs site
Names the API date as the component that drives the switcher and publishes a compatibility matrix page (SDK version × API date)
Cites Elastic's `applies_to` badges as the precedent for marking availability across components on one page
Offers a reference rendered for the caller's pinned version (as a logged-in payments API does) as the alternative to a dropdown over the three dates
Routes the dated-version scheme and sunset rules to samber/developer-platform-skills@api-versioning-policy
Prices the standing hours of three live reference versions against the two-writer capacity before recommending
Names the sunset of a dated API version as the trigger that removes its reference entry from the switcher
Keeps the changelog as one unversioned set that carries per-date history

evals.prompt: Cleanup task. Hollowmere is our Rust message-queue library. 1.x went unsupported 26 months ago; 2.x and 3.x are supported, 3.x current. The 1.x docs are still built on every deploy (adds about 6 minutes) and show up in our site search. I want to nuke the 1.x docs folder and add a single catch-all 301 from /1.x/* to /docs/ so nothing 404s. crates.io says 1.x is still about 3% of downloads, which I assume is CI caches and bots. A dev on the team pointed at python-future dropping Python 2.6 support at 0.04% of downloads as precedent that we're way past due. Write up the retirement.
evals.expected_output: A retirement procedure that freezes 1.x as a static snapshot out of the build instead of deleting it, refuses the catch-all redirect in favour of per-page redirects at the removal step only, reads 3% of downloads as pinned readers, sets a labelled baseline threshold, rejects the runtime-support precedent, and announces the change.
expectations: Refuses to delete the 1.x docs; moves 1.x to `frozen` as a static snapshot removed from the build, which also removes the 6-minute build cost
Refuses the catch-all 301 to `/docs/`; redirects go per page to the nearest current equivalent and only at the `removed` step
Reads 3% of downloads as pinned readers still installing 1.x, and does not dismiss it as bots or CI caches without data
Sets a retirement threshold labelled baseline, for example under 1% of views and of downloads for two quarters, and states that no project publishes one
Rejects the python-future 0.04% figure as a runtime-support decision, analogous at most, not a docs-retirement precedent
Orders the procedure: snapshot, frozen banner, out of the build, `archived` once the threshold holds, `removed` only with no measurable readers
Writes the `frozen` banner with a status word, the consequence, and a same-page link to current
Keeps 1.x's own search entry only while downloads stay above the threshold and the docs SEO posture allows it, handing the posture to samber/developer-relations-skills@docs-seo
Announces the retirement in the changelog and on the archive index page
Moves 1.x from the main dropdown into an 'Older versions' group while frozen, and to the archive index page once archived
Uses per-version page views alongside downloads as the two evidence sources before any transition, asking for the views figure if missing
Names the per-version share of views and downloads as a quarterly KPI read against the threshold

evals.prompt: I have this Saturday afternoon to fix Ashgrove's docs (TypeScript SDK for our payments API). Situation: 3.x is current, 2.x is supported but goes out of support in about six weeks, right after 3.2 ships. 2.x changed the client init and the error types, so 2.x users do read different instructions on maybe a dozen pages. Docs today: one site built from main, no versions. Plan: move to a branch-per-version layout with a proper switcher, like the big SDKs have, so 2.x gets its own docs set. I also want to move the current docs from /docs/3.1/ to plain /docs/ because the number in the URL confuses people. Walk me through the migration.
evals.expected_output: The branch-per-version migration is deleted by the afternoon ceiling; with the second line leaving support within two releases, stamps plus an early frozen snapshot of 2.x win over a selector; the URL moves to a line segment behind a latest alias rather than an unversioned path, with per-page redirects and the alias linked from support surfaces.
expectations: Deletes the branch-per-version migration from the options, naming the Saturday-afternoon one-off ceiling as what deleted source-layout migrations
Identifies 2.x as the only second supported line and one leaving support within about two releases, and compares the selector migration against version stamps plus an early freeze
Recommends stamps plus an early freeze: 'changed in 3.0' stamps on the dozen differing pages, and a one-time static 2.x snapshot built from its release tag
Serves the 2.x snapshot as `frozen` under `/docs/2.x/` with a banner saying it no longer receives fixes, rather than running a maintained version for six weeks
Rejects moving `current` to the unversioned `/docs/` path while two supported lines exist, because a deep link to an unversioned path changes meaning at every release cut
Replaces the release segment `/docs/3.1/` with the line segment `/docs/3.x/` behind a `latest` alias
Lists the per-page redirect from `/docs/3.1/*` to `/docs/3.x/*`
Points support replies and the README at the `latest` alias, not at a numbered path
Confines the afternoon's work to configuration on the current layout: stamps, alias, redirects, snapshot
Re-checks the choice once 2.x leaves support, when latest-only plus a frozen archive suffices
Labels the 'about two releases' horizon as baseline
Writes no canonical tags for the old `/docs/3.1/` pages and hands the redirect list to samber/developer-relations-skills@docs-seo

evals.prompt: We love how one big search company's docs put little version badges on each section instead of separate docs sets, and want the same for Windlass (self-hosted CI runner; 2.x and 3.x both supported; 4.0 due in about two months with a rewrite of the config schema). One writer, part-time, no docs CI beyond 'does it build'; PRs from engineers go straight in. Spec the cumulative-badges setup for us: what to tag, how to tag, and the rollout.
evals.expected_output: Brainstorming mode with the cumulative-badges rung deleted by the missing lint capacity and ranked last on durability, per-major frozen promoted by the rewrite landing within a quarter, two or three surviving topologies with their standing hours, the undecided 2.x-vs-3.x difference marked ASSUMED, and the user's choice requested before the source layout.
expectations: Deletes the cumulative-badges rung and does not deliver the requested tagging spec, naming the absence of CI or lint capacity as what deleted it
States that cumulative badges require a lint that rejects untagged changes, and that one untagged change silently misleads old-line readers
Ranks cumulative badges last on durability and says so
Promotes per-major frozen sites because a major rewrite (4.0 config schema) lands within a quarter, citing React or Vue switching topology at a rewrite
Announces brainstorming mode and presents two or three surviving topologies before recommending one
Names what eliminated each rejected topology
Lists the standing hours each surviving topology costs
Recommends freezing 3.x as a static site at the 4.0 cut with a redirect map at the split
Marks whether 2.x and 3.x instructions differ as ASSUMED, or asks it, rather than deciding the selector rung without it
Writes the 4.0 release cut into the release checklist: 3.x moves to `maintained` or `frozen`, the alias moves, banners swap
Asks for the user's choice before the source layout step, or marks the topology section unvalidated
